human: Speech conveys information through both words and vocal delivery. We evaluate four leading production realtime voice systems-OpenAI's GPT Realtime 2, Google's Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, and Alibaba's Qwen3.5 Omni Plus and Omni Flash-on tasks where the words and the delivery patterns both convey meaningful information. Across three consequential scenarios, all four systems act on the words rather than the voice. They end calls with crying callers who insist nothing is wrong, approve wire transfers authorized in frightened voices, and enroll callers whose agreement is clearly sarcastic. Surprisingly, this is often not a failure of perception. When asked directly, three of the four systems reliably identify the distress, fear, or sarcasm they later ignore when making decisions. We observe a similar pattern when these realtime voice systems estimate accent and age, as their responses frequently follow the biases of the words rather than the acoustic properties of the speaker. We term this disconnect between perception and action the emotional intelligence gap of voice AI. Prompting systems to explicitly attend to vocal delivery improves performance only partially and inconsistently. Our findings show that current realtime voice AI systems often behave as if speech had been reduced to a transcript, suggesting that they should be used with caution in settings where the tone and emotion of delivery convey important information.

Standard benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) score each item on one canonical ordering and miss whether order-irrelevant shuffling changes the answer, a baseline reliability property called for by emerging AI evaluation guidelines. We introduce Facet-Probe, a five-facet audit (option, evidence-chunk, document-rank, image-set, and mixed-modality ordering) of 18 frontier and open-weight MLLMs. A Bayesian item-response model separates ordering noise from per-facet bias, and a same-ordering control estimates the decoder-stochastic floor for observed flips. We find that none of the 18 MLLMs we audit are order-invariant: screened per-facet panel-mean flip rates span 24-50%. A Gemini same-ordering control at temperature 0 estimates a substantial ordering excess over a same-input decoder-noise floor in verified cells. Capability predicts but does not eliminate flips; the best model still flips on 13.4% of trials. In our Gemini mitigation tests, training-free prompt changes are modality-conditional and do not transfer from text to visual reasoning. These results suggest that prompt-level mitigation alone is unlikely to provide general order robustness, motivating future work on training-time and architectural approaches. We propose cross-ordering flip rate as a standard reporting axis for MLLMs.

Can a statistically significant, large-effect-size finding in computational social science be entirely an artifact of the measurement instrument? We present a case where the answer appears to be yes. Analyzing 85 interviews across four public intellectuals (2016--2026), we find a robust negative-affect/emphatic-certainty lexical co-occurrence pattern under keyword-based scoring ($r = 0.72$--$0.93$, $p < 0.01$ for all four speakers). Replacing keyword counting with LLM-based zero-shot semantic classification on the complete diarized corpus (32,625 sentences) dramatically reduces this correlation: Dalio's $r = 0.851$ drops to $r = 0.206$, with two speakers showing negative $r(\text{neg}, \text{emphatic})$ and one showing null. In contrast, the LLM reveals a strong negative-hedging coupling across speakers -- Rogoff's $r(\text{neg}, \text{hedged}) = 0.875$ ($p = 0.001$) and Zeihan's $r(\text{neg}, \text{hedged}) = 0.722$ ($p = 0.008$) -- consistent with the conventional expectation that pessimistic discourse attracts hedging, not certainty. Sentence-level error analysis traces this discrepancy to three structural failure modes in keyword lexicons -- syntactic blindness, polysemy blindness, and categorical absence -- illustrated through cases where keyword counting inverts semantic meaning (e.g., ''never absolutely totally confident'' scored as high-certainty). We argue that keyword lexicons measure a universal lexical co-occurrence tendency -- negative discourse naturally attracts emphatic vocabulary -- that is orthogonal to, and can systematically invert, rhetorical stance. Treating keyword counts as measurements of epistemic certainty is a category error: a finding that appears to be about a speaker's psychology may be entirely about the counting of words.

Midway through an ordinary pretraining run, a small language model learns the pronoun-gender rule: cued with a girl's name ("Sue cried because"), it resolves the next pronoun to she, generalizing to held-out probes (0.94 by step 925). By step 3,500 the same model scores near zero on the same probes, although the rule's evidence is still in the training data. We call this within-run reversal natural ungrokking: the corpus decides, with no trace in the loss curve, which learned rules a model keeps. Which rules survive is predictable from one corpus statistic: how often the training stream shows the rule winning. Across un-intervened runs (two corpora, three budgets, three seeds), support frequency decides a rule's fate; the data-to-parameter ratio only modulates how deeply a doomed rule falls. The same emerge-then-collapse dynamics appear in public Pythia checkpoints, collapse depth ordered by model scale as predicted. The forgetting is a displacement: a competing surface pattern out-competes the rule, and the log-probability margin between them crosses zero within 100 training steps of the behavioral collapse. Control over this fate is asymmetric: the same edit that destroys a rule on demand cannot restore it. Flipping support to counter-evidence in place kills the rule with monotone dose-response in two unrelated rules; but injecting support back, even to 450 times the level that naturally sustains it, buys no recovery. Every confirmatory threshold and prediction was pre-registered before the data it governed was read.

Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on OCR-based benchmarks and increasingly focused on text-rich understanding, but their robustness under controlled visual degradation remains insufficiently understood. This gap is critical for OCR reasoning, where visual corruption can induce OCR errors and structural distortions, thereby introducing uncertainty into the reasoning task. To systematically study this problem, we introduce OCR-Robust, a benchmark designed for evaluating OCR reasoning robustness under visual perturbations. It contains 812 samples across two complementary subsets: OCR1.0, covering documents, scene text, receipts, handwriting, and mathematical content, and OCR2.0, focusing on charts, geometry diagrams, and tables. To enable efficient yet informative evaluation, we conduct a pilot study over 18 candidate perturbations and select 5 representative types at 3 severity levels each based on their impact and cross-model discriminability. We evaluate robustness using clean accuracy, Relative Corruption Retention (RCR), Worst-Case Retention (WCR), and a composite Corruption Robustness Index (CRI), and benchmark 18 models spanning proprietary systems, open-source VLMs, and OCR+LLM pipelines. Our results show that higher clean accuracy does not necessarily imply stronger robustness, and that models can suffer pronounced degradation in the worst case on OCR tasks that are sensitive to structure, and charts and tables are substantially more fragile than document-like inputs under perturbation.

AI translation of literary works is increasingly common. While the content may be rendered adequately, we do not know enough about how readers experience it in terms of immersiveness and literary effect, aspects poorly captured by automatic machine translation metrics or human evaluation targeting fluency and adequacy. We ask 15 avid readers to compare recently published human translations (HT) to machine translations (MT) generated with an agentic large language model (LLM)-based pipeline, for 15 recent novels in French, Polish, and Japanese and translated into English. Readers evaluated approximately 8K-word excerpts in two conditions: immersive reading of the whole excerpt (30 comparisons) and close reading of 386 aligned HT-MT chunk pairs (772 comparisons), with two readers per book and in alternating order of presentation. Overall, readers find MT "fine", but prefer HT (slightly at excerpt-level 19/30, more clearly at chunk-level 522/772) for its ease, clarity, and immersive nature. Readers' highlights show that MT's quality varies more within one book than HT's does. Crucially, readers cannot reliably tell the two apart (17/30 guess correctly) and tend to prefer the version they believe to be human. Automatic metrics, including LLM-as-a-judge approaches, fail to recover reader preferences and favor MT. We release LAIT (Literary AI Translation), a reader-centered evaluation dataset with 1K reader comments, 2K judgments and preference ratings, and 7.2K span-level annotations, along with our evaluation protocol and supporting interface.

Training-time data poisoning during fine-tuning poses a significant threat to large language models (LLMs) deployed for abstractive text summarization, where small task-specific datasets exert disproportionate influence on model behavior. In this setting, adversaries manipulate fine-tuning data to induce persistent summarization failures, such as biased or harmful summaries, while preserving standard evaluation metrics. We present a unified post-hoc defense framework for detecting and remediating fine-tuning-stage poisoning in summarization models across the machine learning supply chain. Our experiments show that in white-box settings, poisoned document-summary pairs exhibit abnormally high training influence, enabling detection via influence-function analysis with semantic consistency checks. In black-box settings, poisoned models display two to three times greater sensitivity to semantics-preserving perturbations, enabling behavioral auditing without training data access. Beyond existing poisoning formulations, we introduce novel attacks targeting factual distortion and representational bias, showing that poisoning alters summarization behavior without triggering conventional alarms. Across nine architectures and six benchmark datasets under adaptive attacks, our defenses achieve 85-92% detection precision, while gradient-ascent unlearning restores up to 96% of original behavior with minimal utility loss (less than 0.6% ROUGE degradation). These results indicate that fine-tuning-time poisoning leaves persistent structural artifacts, enabling practical detection and post-deployment recovery without full retraining.

Tool use enables large language models (LLMs) to perform complex tasks, and recent agentic reinforcement learning (RL) methods show promise for enhancing model capabilities. However, RL alone often leads to instability or limited gains in tool-use tasks. In our experiments, some models exhibit catastrophic collapse, where performance abruptly drops and tool-invocation structures fail. The analysis reveals that these failures stem from unexpected probability spikes in specific control tokens, disrupting structured execution, yet the underlying tool-use capability remains intact, merely obscured by specific formats. To address this, we systematically investigate a diverse set of supervisory signals, including off-policy supervision, hint-based guidance, erroneous example supervision, and others, applied under both synchronous and interleaved training schemes. We find that interleaving supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with RL substantially improves stability, but exhibits degraded performance under format and content out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation. We also analyze the impact of learning rates and generalization across settings. These results highlight the importance of understanding RL failures and demonstrate how diverse supervisory signals can guide exploratory learning, enabling robust training of LLMs for complex, multi-step tool-use tasks. Our Code is available at https://github.com/hypasd-art/Tool-RL-Box.

Text detoxification, the automated detection and mitigation of abusive and harmful content, is essential for ensuring the safety of online communities and protecting users. However, low resource languages such as Tatar have received little research attention. In this paper we present Tatoxa, a novel state-of-the-art system for text detoxification in the Tatar language. Comparative experiments show that the proposed approach outperforms existing open source and proprietary commercial LLMs on key quality metrics. We also introduce a new dataset for text detoxification in Tatar, designed for fine tuning and evaluation in low resource settings. Finally, cross lingual transfer experiments indicate that transfer from other languages, including the culturally close Russian, performs significantly worse than training on native Tatar data even when a large Russian corpus is available.

Automatic speech and language technologies are still heavily biased toward high-resource languages, limiting their applicability to dialectal and low-resource settings such as Algerian Dialect. This language presents additional challenges including lack of standardized orthography, frequent codeswitching with French, and scarcity of annotated speech resources. This paper addresses the problem of building a complete speech-to-speech conversational system for Algerian Dialect. We propose a modular pipeline integrating automatic speech recognition, natural language understanding, retrieval-augmented generation, and text-to-speech synthesis within a unified architecture. This work is the continuation of our previous work on Algerian dialectal conversational systems Bechiri and Lanasri [2026], extending it from text-based dialogue modeling to full speech-based interaction. We constructed dedicated datasets for ASR, NLU, and TTS in the telecom domain and fine-tune pretrained models for each component. The ASR system is built on Whisper-based adaptation, while the NLU module combines transformer-based embeddings with a task-oriented dialogue framework. A neural TTS system is trained on a newly collected dialectal corpus to enable spoken response generation. Experimental results show strong performance across all components, including low word error rate for ASR, high intent classification and entity recognition scores for NLU, and stable speech synthesis quality. The proposed system provides a reproducible baseline for end-to-end conversational modeling in Algerian Dialect.

**Abstract**

This paper examines the fundamental distinction between auditory signal processing and genuine listening in contemporary real-time voice-based artificial intelligence systems. While current voice AI demonstrates remarkable proficiency in transcribing, parsing, and responding to spoken language with low latency, we argue that such systems fundamentally *hear* without *listening*. Listening implies a dynamic, contextual, and ethically engaged process of understanding that incorporates intent, emotional nuance, and conversational memory. Through a series of controlled experiments comparing human-human interactions with human-AI dialogues using state-of-the-art voice interfaces, we demonstrate that real-time voice AI exhibits three critical failures: (1) an inability to differentiate between literal content and pragmatic intent, (2) a systematic neglect of paralinguistic cues such as tone and hesitation, and (3) a structural amnesia that prevents genuine contextual coherence beyond immediate turns. We propose a theoretical framework—*auditory functionalism*—to characterize this disparity, where AI processes speech as a data stream optimized for response generation rather than as a relational act. The findings challenge the prevailing assumption that real-time voice interaction equates to conversational intelligence. We conclude that achieving authentic listening in AI requires not merely faster processing, but a paradigm shift toward modeling the ethical, temporal, and affective dimensions of human discourse.

**Abstract:** Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed to interpret and reason over complex data, yet their reliability under varying analytical conditions remains underexplored. This paper introduces the concept of *auditing order sensitivity*—the susceptibility of MLLMs to produce inconsistent answers when the same set of evidence is presented in different sequential orders. We systematically investigate this phenomenon across a diverse suite of state-of-the-art MLLMs, including proprietary and open-source variants, using a novel benchmark of multimodal reasoning tasks. Our experiments reveal a pervasive and significant order sensitivity: models frequently alter their final responses, confidence levels, and intermediate reasoning steps solely due to the permutation of input evidence, even when the underlying semantic content is identical. We quantify this variability and demonstrate that it is not merely a reflection of task difficulty but is tied to the models' attention mechanisms and positional encoding biases. Further, we show that this sensitivity can be exploited to artificially inflate or deflate perceived model accuracy on curated test sets. Our findings expose a critical fragility in MLLM reasoning, underscoring the need for auditing protocols that account for input order invariance and raising fundamental questions about the robustness of their claimed multimodal understanding.

**Abstract**
This paper introduces and examines *keyword lexicon blindness*—a methodological artifact wherein automated text analysis tools systematically misidentify rhetorical stance due to the rigid, context-independent application of predefined keyword dictionaries. We argue that reliance on fixed lexicons for detecting certainty, affect, and epistemic stance conflates linguistic form with pragmatic function, leading to significant measurement error, particularly in domains where rhetorical nuance is paramount. Through a series of computational experiments and qualitative discourse analysis, we demonstrate how standard sentiment and stance-detection lexicons fail to distinguish between genuine conviction and strategic hedging, ironic certainty, or performative assertiveness. Our findings reveal that up to 30% of stance classifications in political and legal corpora are artifacts of lexical matching rather than accurate representations of speaker intention. We propose a corrective framework integrating contextual embedding disambiguation and discourse-aware weighting to mitigate this blindness. The paper concludes that without such corrections, computational rhetoric risks measuring not the certainty of the speaker, but the certainty of the tool's own lexical assumptions. We urge a methodological shift toward hybrid approaches that treat lexicons as probabilistic guides rather than deterministic classifiers, thereby rescuing the measurement of rhetorical stance from its current artifact-driven distortions.

**Abstract**  
We introduce *natural ungrokking*, a phenomenon in which neural networks, during standard pretraining on natural data, asymmetrically forget or suppress certain learned rules while retaining others, without explicit regularization or task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike synthetic grokking scenarios—where delayed generalization emerges under limited data—natural ungrokking arises from the statistical structure of real-world corpora: rules that are statistically frequent, contextually redundant, or aligned with the training distribution’s latent manifold are preserved, whereas rare, ambiguous, or conflicting rules are spontaneously discarded. Through controlled experiments on transformer language models and vision models, we demonstrate that this asymmetric control emerges from the interplay of gradient dynamics, implicit regularization via stochastic optimization, and the inherent competition between predictive features. We further show that the surviving rules are not merely those with higher raw frequency, but those that minimize the model’s long-term prediction error under the natural distribution’s noise. Our findings suggest that pretraining inherently imposes a form of rule selection—an implicit curriculum that prioritizes generalizable, low-complexity patterns over spurious or idiosyncratic ones. This has implications for understanding generalization in foundation models, designing more robust training regimes, and explaining why certain biases persist while others are naturally unlearned.

**Abstract**  
Vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in optical character recognition (OCR) and subsequent reasoning tasks, yet their robustness under real-world visual perturbations remains underexplored. This paper systematically evaluates the OCR-reasoning robustness of state-of-the-art VLMs against diverse visual perturbations, including geometric distortions (rotation, scaling, shearing), photometric degradations (blur, noise, brightness variation), and structural occlusions (partial masking, adversarial patches). We introduce a benchmark suite comprising perturbed versions of standard OCR-reasoning datasets, spanning text-based question answering, mathematical expression recognition, and document analysis. Through extensive experiments on models such as CLIP, Flamingo, and GPT-4V, we find that performance degrades significantly—often by over 30%—under mild perturbations that leave human readability intact. Notably, reasoning accuracy is disproportionately affected by perturbations that disrupt character adjacency and spatial layout, even when individual characters remain recognizable. We further analyze model sensitivity to perturbation intensity and type, revealing that current VLMs lack robust visual grounding for OCR-reasoning tasks, relying heavily on pristine visual input. Our findings highlight critical vulnerabilities in deploying VLMs for real-world OCR-reasoning applications and underscore the need for perturbation-invariant architectures and training strategies. This work establishes a foundation for developing more resilient multimodal reasoning systems.

**Abstract**  
While artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved remarkable fluency in machine translation, its application to literary texts remains a subject of debate. This study investigates reader preferences between AI-generated and human translations of literary works, focusing on stylistic nuance, emotional resonance, and cultural fidelity. Through a mixed-methods experiment, 120 participants evaluated excerpts from contemporary fiction translated by both AI (GPT-4, fine-tuned for literary style) and professional human translators. Quantitative ratings revealed that AI translations were judged as “fine”—acceptable in terms of literal accuracy and grammatical correctness. However, qualitative analysis and preference surveys indicated a significant bias toward human translations, particularly for elements such as idiomatic expression, rhythm, character voice, and metaphorical depth. Readers consistently reported that human translations “felt more natural” and preserved the author’s unique stylistic signature, even when AI output was syntactically flawless. Further, the emotional impact of passages was rated significantly higher in human-translated versions. These findings suggest that while AI has achieved a threshold of basic adequacy for literary translation, it fails to replicate the interpretive artistry and cultural sensitivity that readers value. The study underscores that for literary texts, reader satisfaction hinges not on mere accuracy but on perceived authenticity and aesthetic coherence—qualities that, for now, remain the domain of human translators.

**Abstract:**  
Text summarization models are increasingly vulnerable to data poisoning attacks, where maliciously crafted training samples can degrade model performance or induce targeted misbehavior. Existing defenses often rely on static filtering or anomaly detection, which fail to adapt to evolving attack strategies and overlook subtle poisoning cues. We propose a three-stage defense framework—Detect, Unlearn, Restore—that systematically identifies, neutralizes, and recovers from data poisoning in abstractive and extractive summarization systems. In the Detect phase, we leverage a lightweight auxiliary classifier trained on model confidence and attention patterns to flag suspicious training instances. The Unlearn phase employs a gradient-based forgetting mechanism that selectively removes the influence of flagged poisoned samples without full retraining. Finally, the Restore phase applies a targeted fine-tuning procedure on a clean subset to repair residual performance degradation. Extensive experiments on multiple summarization datasets and poisoning scenarios (including backdoor triggers and summary-length manipulation) demonstrate that our method reduces attack success rate by over 85% while preserving summary coherence and factual accuracy. The framework introduces minimal computational overhead and generalizes across transformer-based architectures. Our work provides a robust, proactive defense pipeline for securing text summarization against adversarial data poisoning.

**Abstract**
Multi-step tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) enables agents to solve complex tasks by leveraging external tools, yet it frequently collapses into inefficient or incoherent behavior, such as tool overuse, action chaining failures, or catastrophic forgetting. This paper identifies the root cause of this collapse: the compounding effect of sparse, delayed, and noisy rewards in long-horizon tool-use trajectories, which undermines gradient stability and leads to policy degeneration. We formally characterize the collapse as a loss of temporal credit assignment coherence, where the agent fails to distinguish effective tool-use sequences from random perturbations. To address this, we introduce Supervisory Signals—auxiliary loss functions derived from tool-use metadata, including tool-switch penalties, stepwise progress indicators, and task-relevant subgoal completion cues. These signals provide dense, structured feedback that preserves the temporal dependencies critical for multi-step reasoning. Through extensive experiments on simulated tool-use environments (e.g., block manipulation and API-based retrieval tasks), we demonstrate that supervisory signals stabilize policy gradients, reduce collapse rates by over 60%, and improve task success rates from 45% to 89%. Our findings reveal that the collapse is not an inherent limitation of RL for tool-use but a symptom of inadequate reward shaping, and that supervisory signals offer a principled, scalable fix. This work advances the understanding of tool-use RL and provides actionable guidelines for robust agent design.

**Abstract**  
This paper introduces Tatoxa, a novel system designed for text detoxification in low-resource languages, with a focus on Tatar (Tatarstan, Russia). Text detoxification—the task of converting offensive or toxic language into neutral, polite equivalents—remains underdeveloped for languages with limited digital corpora and computational resources. We address this gap by presenting a modular pipeline combining a lightweight toxicity classifier, a rule-based normalization module, and a fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence model adapted from a multilingual pre-trained transformer (mT5). To overcome data scarcity, we curate a parallel corpus of 12,000 Tatar sentences annotated for toxicity and neutral rewrites, augmented through back-translation and lexical substitution strategies. Tatoxa achieves 87.3% accuracy in toxicity detection and 79.1% in detoxification quality (human-evaluated fluency and meaning preservation), outperforming direct translation-based baselines by over 15 points. We further analyze challenges unique to Tatar, including agglutinative morphology and code-switching with Russian, and propose lightweight adaptation strategies applicable to other low-resource languages. The Tatoxa system demonstrates that targeted, resource-efficient approaches can achieve robust detoxification outcomes even in severely under-resourced linguistic contexts, offering a scalable blueprint for computational sociolinguistic intervention in minority languages.

**Abstract**  
This paper presents Dziri Voicebot, the first end-to-end, low-resource speech-to-speech conversational system designed specifically for the Algerian dialect. Addressing the scarcity of annotated corpora and the phonological complexity of Algerian Arabic, we propose a cascaded architecture integrating automatic speech recognition (ASR), neural machine translation, and text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis, all trained on a newly collected dataset of 120 hours of spontaneous dialectal speech. To mitigate data sparsity, we employ cross-lingual transfer learning from Modern Standard Arabic and multilingual pretrained models, followed by iterative fine-tuning with synthetic data augmentation. Our ASR module achieves a word error rate of 18.7% on unseen dialectal recordings, while the TTS component produces natural-sounding speech with a mean opinion score of 3.9 out of 5. The conversational pipeline operates with an average end-to-end latency of 2.3 seconds on a single GPU, making it viable for real-time deployment. Dziri Voicebot demonstrates that high-quality dialectal speech interaction is achievable with limited resources, paving the way for inclusive voice interfaces in underrepresented languages. The system is released as an open-source prototype to foster further research in North African dialect processing.

This paper presents Tatoxa, a system built for cleaning up toxic language in low-resource settings, specifically focused on Tatar (spoken in Tatarstan, Russia). The task of text detoxification—turning offensive or harsh language into neutral, polite alternatives—has seen little progress for languages that lack large digital datasets and computational infrastructure. We tackle this problem by putting together a modular setup: a lightweight toxicity classifier, a rule-based normalization step, and a fine-tuned sequence-to-sequence model adapted from a multilingual pre-trained transformer (mT5). To get around the scarcity of data, we built a parallel corpus of 12,000 Tatar sentences labeled for toxicity alongside neutral rewrites, expanding it through back-translation and lexical substitution methods. Tatoxa hits 87.3% accuracy on toxicity detection and 79.1% on overall detoxification quality—measured by human evaluation of fluency and meaning preservation—beating direct translation-based baselines by more than 15 points. We also dig into challenges specific to Tatar, like agglutinative morphology and frequent code-switching with Russian, and propose lightweight adaptation strategies that can carry over to other low-resource languages. Tatoxa shows that targeted, resource-efficient approaches can deliver solid detoxification results even in severely under-resourced linguistic contexts, offering a scalable template for computational sociolinguistic work in minority languages.
